**The Keeper of Stonewrack Point**

Elias Marrow had tended the lighthouse at Stonewrack Point for thirty-one years, and in all that time, he had never once watched it from the water. He had seen it from the catwalk, from the gallery, from the rocky shelf where he gathered mussels at low tide, but never from a boat looking back toward shore, the way the sailors saw it. That was about to change, though not by his choosing.

The storm had come up fast, the way October storms did on this stretch of coast, with a sky that had been merely grey at noon turning the color of a day-old bruise by four. Elias had been down at the village, collecting his monthly stores and a letter from his daughter in the city, when the wind shifted and the first hard gusts came off the water like something angry had been let loose. By the time he reached the dock, old Tomlin's boat was the only one still out, and Tomlin himself, half-deaf and stubborn as a barnacle, was somewhere beyond the point checking his lobster pots.

"He won't hear the horn," said Birdie Hask, who ran the bait shop and had eyes sharper than anyone twice her age. "He never does till he's right under it."

Elias looked out at the water, already churning white at the edges, and did not think very long before he was in his own small boat, the one he used for errands along the shore, pulling the cord on the outboard motor with hands that remembered how even though his mind told him this was foolish.

The lighthouse was behind him now, and that was the strange part, the part he turned over even as he fought the tiller. Thirty-one years he had climbed its hundred and twelve steps every evening at dusk, had trimmed the great lamp's wick in the days before it was electric, had polished the brass fittings until his own face looked back at him warped and golden. He knew that tower the way another man might know his wife's face, every joint of stone, every place where the mortar had been repointed, the exact sound the door made when the wind caught it wrong. But he had never seen it as a sailor saw it, small and far and the only thing standing between a man and the rocks.

Now, with the boat bucking under him and spray stinging his eyes, he looked back, and there it was: the beam sweeping its slow arc across the water, patient as a held breath, indifferent to the storm in the way that only something built for exactly this purpose could be indifferent. It did not know fear. It simply turned, and turned, and turned, because that was what it was for.

He understood, in that moment, something he had never quite put into words in three decades of solitary evenings. The lighthouse was not for the calm nights. On calm nights it was almost an ornament, a pretty thing that blinked at the stars. It was built, every stone of it, for nights exactly like this one, and so was he. He had taken the job at twenty-six because his wife had just died and the thought of silence had seemed, then, like the only mercy available to him. He had stayed eight years past when he might have retired because the rhythm of it—the climbing, the polishing, the keeping—had become the shape of his days, and he hadn't known how to be a man without that shape. But he had never, not once, thought of himself as necessary in the way the tower was necessary. He had thought of himself as its attendant. Now, bent low against the wind with Tomlin's boat nowhere yet in sight, he understood he had been wrong. He was not the tower's servant. He was its twin.

He found Tomlin twenty minutes later, closer to the rocks than any sane man would risk even in fair weather, hauling a pot with the stubbornness of someone who had decided the storm was a rumor and not a fact. Elias throttled down, shouted until his voice cracked, and when that failed, he did what he always swore he would never do again after the accident that took two fingers on his left hand some years back: he came in close, close enough to throw a line, close enough that a wrong swell could have put both boats on the rocks together.

"You're a damned fool, Tomlin!" he bellowed, when the old lobsterman finally looked up, startled, as if he'd forgotten the rest of the world existed.

"Pot's full," Tomlin shouted back, grinning with the gaps where his back teeth used to be, and Elias had the brief, mad urge to laugh, because of course that was the answer, of course a man who'd spend his whole life wringing a living from this coast would not abandon a full pot for something as trivial as a gale.

It took the better part of an hour to get them both back around the point, the lighthouse beam sweeping over them again and again, a kind of metronome against which Elias measured the distance left to go. He found himself talking to it, under his breath, the way he sometimes did on long nights alone in the lamp room. Not out loud, not in any way a man would admit to another man, but there, nonetheless. *Hold on,* he told it. *I'm coming back.* As if the tower might, in his absence, forget how to do the one thing it had always done.

When they finally rounded into the lee of the point and the water calmed to something merely rough instead of murderous, Elias looked up at Stonewrack from below for the first time in thirty-one years. From here it did not look small at all. It looked impossibly tall, a white spear driven up out of black rock, and the light at its crown swept over him like a hand laid briefly on his shoulder before moving on to sweep the water beyond, because that was its job, and its job did not stop for one tired keeper and one foolish lobsterman making their way home.

Birdie had a fire going in the bait shop stove by the time they got Tomlin's boat secured, and she poured something dark and medicinal into two chipped mugs without being asked. Tomlin drank his in one go and went off grumbling about the lost hour, already more concerned with his pots than with the fact that he had nearly died.

Elias sat a while longer, mug warming his hands, and watched through the salt-fogged window as the light kept turning above the village, steady, patient, unbothered by what it had just witnessed or failed to witness. In an hour he would climb the hundred and twelve steps again, as he did every evening, and check the lamp, and polish what needed polishing, and make his quiet rounds. Nothing about his routine would change. But something in how he understood it had shifted, the way a stone shifts half an inch in its socket and settles into a truer fit.

He was not the keeper of the light. He had told himself that story for thirty-one years because it was easier than the truth, which was that the light had kept him, had given his grief a shape to pour itself into, had turned his solitary life into something that mattered to sailors he would never meet, moving through darkness he would never see from their side of it. Tonight, for one hour, he had seen it from their side. He did not think he would forget it.

Outside, the storm was already breaking apart, the way October storms always did, spending their fury fast and leaving behind a sky scrubbed raw and clean.
